faq.q: What are good games for people with dementia?
faq.a: Good games are simple, familiar and free of pressure: large pictures to match, sorting, easy jigsaws, finishing well-known sayings, coloring, picture bingo and conversation cards. The best choice is the one the person enjoys today. Avoid timers, scores and anything that feels like a test.
Yes. Every game and printable on Golden Moments is free, with no account, sign-up or download. The games run in the web browser on a phone, tablet or computer.

No game has been shown to prevent dementia, and Golden Moments does not claim to treat or prevent anything. Our games are for enjoyment and time together. Our brain health section explains what research does and does not show.

faq.q: Are these games suitable for someone with Alzheimer's?
faq.a: Yes. Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia, and the games are made for it: large pictures that stay showing, few choices, and nothing to remember or get wrong. Matching, sorting and finishing familiar sayings lean on long-held knowledge rather than new learning.

faq.q: Can someone with later-stage dementia use these activities?
faq.a: Often, yes, with someone beside them. Start with Find the same with two pictures, Picture pairs with four tiles, a coloring page or a calm breathing pause. Keep it short, follow their lead and stop when they have had enough.

about.title: A Shared Activity, Not a Memory Test
about.description: Why Golden Moments games have no timers, scores or streaks, why pictures stay showing, and what we will and will not claim about dementia.
about.lede: Golden Moments makes calm, adult picture activities that a caregiver and someone living with dementia can enjoy side by side.
about.bodyHtml:
What we believe

The point of an activity is the moment itself: a conversation, a smile, the satisfaction of putting two pictures together, or simply sitting close. It is not to measure anyone, push them further or prove anything.

Many brain-training apps are designed around speed, scores, streaks and levels. For a person living with dementia that can feel like an exam they cannot pass. We designed the opposite, and we hold ourselves to these rules:

  • Nothing to fail. No clock, score, move counter, lives, streaks, confetti or countdowns, on any screen.
  • Recognition over recall. Pictures stay showing by default. Prompts invite conversation and never quiz names or memories.
  • Big, plain and steady. Large text and pictures, high contrast, and controls that stay in the same place.
  • Adult dignity. Real-world pictures and plain, warm words. No cartoons, sing-song praise or emoji rewards.
  • An easy way out. “Done for now” is always visible. Stopping halfway is a good outcome.
  • Private by default. No accounts or ads. Photos you choose stay on your device.

What we do not claim

Our games are for enjoyment and connection. They do not diagnose, test, measure, treat, slow or prevent dementia or Alzheimer’s disease, and no one should choose them for that reason. When we write about research on our brain health pages, we say plainly where the evidence is weak, and we never connect it to our own games.

Who we are

Golden Moments is a small independent team. We are not clinicians. Our guides are written from published guidance by organizations such as the National Institute on Aging and the Alzheimer’s Association, and every guide lists its sources. Read how we write and check our pages.

Tell us what would help

We would love to hear what works for you and what does not, especially from people living with dementia, family caregivers and activity staff. Email {email}.

editorial.title: How We Write and Check Our Pages
editorial.description: How Golden Moments researches, writes, sources and updates its dementia activity and brain health pages, and what we will never publish.
editorial.bodyHtml:
Our sources

We base our guides on public guidance from organizations such as the National Institute on Aging, the CDC, the Alzheimer’s Association, the Alzheimer’s Foundation of America, the Family Caregiver Alliance and the NHS, and on peer-reviewed research such as Cochrane reviews and large clinical trials. Every guide lists the sources it relies on. We open each source before citing it, and we only report what it actually says.

How we write

  • Practical first: what to do today, in plain language.
  • Honest about evidence: we say “linked with”, “may” and “the evidence is mixed” when that is the truth.
  • Respectful: we write about people living with dementia as adults, and we never use quizzing or shaming language.
  • No invented content: no made-up statistics, quotes, experts, studies, reviews or testimonials.

Who reviews our pages

Pages are written and checked by the Golden Moments team, with help from AI writing tools for research and drafting. Every page is checked against its sources by the team. Our pages have not been reviewed by a doctor or other clinician, and we do not claim otherwise. They are general information, not medical advice.

What we will never publish

  • Claims that a game, food, supplement, fast or routine prevents, treats, slows or cures dementia.
  • Tests, quizzes or scores that suggest someone has, or does not have, dementia.
  • Advice to start, stop or change any medicine.
  • Advertising or sponsored content disguised as guidance.

Updates and corrections

Each page shows the date it was last updated. If you find a mistake or an out-of-date source, please email {email} and we will check it promptly.

faq.title: Questions and Answers
faq.seoTitle: Dementia Games and Activities: Questions and Answers
faq.description: Answers to common questions about dementia games and activities: which games to try, how long to play, later-stage ideas, brain health and privacy.
faq.lede: Short, plain answers to the questions caregivers ask most.

items.q: What are the best games for someone with dementia?
items.a: The best games are familiar, simple and free of pressure, and the right one is whatever the person enjoys today. Picture matching with visible pictures, sorting, easy jigsaws, finishing familiar sayings, coloring and picture bingo all work well for many people. Avoid timers, scores and anything that feels like a test.
Yes. All games and printables are free, with no account, sign-up, download or advertising.

items.q: Why are there no scores, levels or timers?
items.a: Speed and scores turn a pleasant activity into an exam, which can bring embarrassment or frustration. We keep the focus on enjoyment and time together, so there is nothing to fail and you can stop at any point.

Any phone, tablet or computer with a modern web browser. A tablet on a stand at a table is often the most comfortable way for two people to play side by side. A laptop connected to a TV works well for groups.

items.q: Can we play with our own family photos?
items.a: Yes. Photo pairs turns 2 to 6 photos you choose into a matching game. The photos stay in your browser and are not uploaded or saved.

items.q: How long should an activity last?
items.a: Often 10 to 20 minutes is plenty, and sometimes 2 minutes is a success. Watch for signs of tiredness or frustration and stop while it still feels good. There is no right amount.

items.q: What if they do not want to do an activity?
items.a: Respect the no, and try again later or in a different way. Refusal can come from tiredness, pain, feeling unsure or simply not being interested. See our guide on what to do when they say no.

Comfort and the senses: listening to favorite music, hand massage with lotion, looking at photos together, holding a soft blanket, sitting outside, or a very simple picture game with someone beside them. Our later-stage guide has many more ideas.

items.q: Are there activities for groups in a care home?
items.a: Yes. Picture bingo has printable cards and an on-screen caller, and Finish the saying and Conversation cards work well read aloud. Our care home groups guide covers group size, seating and adapting for mixed abilities.

items.q: Can games prevent or slow dementia?
items.a: No game has been shown to prevent dementia, and our games make no such claim. Cognitive stimulation in a social setting has shown small benefits in research for people with mild to moderate dementia, but that is different from a game preventing disease. We offer games for enjoyment and connection.

Not with certainty. Research links 14 health and lifestyle factors with dementia risk, such as hearing loss, high blood pressure, physical inactivity and social isolation. Addressing them may lower risk for some people, but many people who do everything right still develop dementia. It is never anyone’s fault.

items.q: Is intermittent fasting good for brain health?
items.a: Human evidence is limited and early, and much of the research is in animals. Fasting can be risky for older adults, especially with diabetes medicines or unintended weight loss, and it is not recommended for people living with dementia. Talk with a doctor before changing how you eat.

No accounts or ads. We use Google Analytics to count visits and see which pages help, and your browser remembers whether you turned soft sounds on. Photos you choose for Photo pairs are never uploaded. See the privacy notice for details.
No. Golden Moments is for recreation and general information. For health questions, talk with a doctor, and for emergencies call 911.

app.title: The Golden Moments App
app.seoTitle: The Golden Moments App for iPhone and Android
app.description: The free Golden Moments app: gentle photo matching with four large tiles, family photos kept on your device, offline picture packs and no account.
app.lede: Everything you like about the website, in an app that works offline and can use family photos you choose.
app.bodyHtml:
Start small

Begin with four large tiles and familiar pictures. Keep pictures visible, or hide them when that feels comfortable. Gentle mode has no timer, score or penalty. Choose 4, 6, 8 or 12 tiles.

Make it personal

Select family photos with your device’s photo picker. The app saves smaller copies for its activities. It does not scan your library or change your original photos, and it keeps up to 24 photos in one collection.

Just look together

View one picture at a time. Optional prompts invite conversation without asking anyone to remember names or give a correct answer. Simply looking is enough.

Offline where it matters

Starter pictures and all eight picture packs are included with the app. Imported photo copies work offline. Choosing originals stored only in iCloud may need an internet connection.

No account, no photo-sync server

Family-photo copies stay in the app on the device. You can remove the copies without deleting originals. Device backups may include app data. Read the app privacy policy, and app help walks through each step.
app.disclaimer: Golden Moments is for recreation and shared conversation. It does not diagnose, treat, prevent or measure dementia or Alzheimer’s disease.

faq.q: Which game should we start with?
faq.a: Picture pairs with four tiles is a calm first choice. If choosing between pictures feels like too much, try Find the same with two pictures. For a group, try Picture bingo.

faq.q: Do the games work on an iPad or phone?
faq.a: Yes. Every game works in the browser on phones, tablets and computers, and the pictures grow to fill the screen. A tablet on a stand is often the most comfortable for two people.

faq.q: Are these games good for someone with Alzheimer's?
faq.a: Yes. They were made for people living with dementia, including Alzheimer's, the most common cause. Pictures stay showing, there are only a few choices, and nothing is timed or scored, so the games lean on recognizing familiar things rather than remembering new ones.

faq.q: Are these memory games for seniors?
faq.a: They are matching and picture games that any older adult can enjoy, but they are built not to test memory: in Picture pairs the pictures stay face up unless you choose otherwise. Our guide to memory games for seniors with dementia explains how to keep any memory game gentle.

faq.q: Are there games for groups in a care home?
faq.a: Yes. Picture bingo has printable cards and an on-screen caller, and Finish the saying and Conversation cards work well read aloud to a group.
